newsitem.title: GERMANY: FORMER USED CAR SALESMAN GRAF LIKED TO BE PAID IN CASH.
newsitem.headline: FORMER USED CAR SALESMAN GRAF LIKED TO BE PAID IN CASH.

text.p: Peter Graf sold second-hand cars before he taught his daughter Steffi to make millions by hitting a ball across a tennis net.
Then he tried to do the tax equivalent of fiddling the mileage clock when it came to declaring the earnings of the women's world number one player and got caught trying to con his country.
A Mannheim court on Friday found Graf guilty of dodging more than 12 million marks ($7 million) in German tax on his daughter's income and sentenced him to three years and nine months in prison.
Tax is a sensitive issue in Germany where most people have seen their bills rise substantially since the country took on the economic burden of former East Germany in 1990.

Graf, who has managed Steffi's financial affairs from her childhood, decided against following sports stars like soccer hero Franz Beckenbauer and Formula One driver Michael Schumacher to a lucrative tax haven.
Instead he bent the rules.

Graf sometimes liked his multi-millionaire daughter to be paid in wads of cash and would leave tournaments with thousands of bank notes stashed in plastic bags, the court heard during the most-publicised tax trial in German history.

What the German media dubbed the "missing millions" of marks (dollars) from prize money and sponsorship contracts were siphoned off through bank accounts in the Netherlands, Liechtenstein and the Dutch Antilles islands in the Caribbean.

Steffi, whose career earnings are estimated at more than $61 million, said she knew very little about the details of her huge wealth and was even unsure how much she made for winning a prestigious event like Wimbledon.
The court said it did not consider her guilty of wrongdoing and recommended authorities stop investigating her.

At times the money must have visited more exotic places than Steffi, who flew around the world making a fortune with the formidable forehand Peter first started to nurture when she was barely bigger than a tennis racket.
Most daughters have a special relationship with their father. But for Steffi, who first picked up a tennis racket as a three-year-old, Peter Graf dominated her life.

He first started tuning Steffi's strokes by battering a ball against the wall for hours in a room in their cellar at home. She was obsessed with the game, her father said, and at six, she won her first tournament.
Two years later Peter gave up selling cars and concentrated all his time on managing her affairs.
Until Graf was arrested in August 1995 and began 15 months behind bars while investigations were carried out and the trial began, the two had virtually been inseparable.

In the early part of her career Peter organised her training, education and marketing. Later he sat in the stands to provide moral support at major tournaments and struck deals with businessmen in the tennis world's ubiquitous VIP tents.
He turned Steffi into the most marketable sportswoman in Germany, advertising everything from pasta to deodorant.

There were times when the player was advised by some of her rivals to enjoy more independence from her father. While Steffi owes a lot to Peter, she has also suffered emotionally because of his actions in the past.
In 1990 her form dipped when stories of Peter Graf's relationship with a nude model were all over the newspapers.
Although she has performed remarkably well in the last two seasons, Steffi has broken down several times in public when asked about the pressure of the tax affair.
Graf's lawyers claimed he got out of his depth and had been led astray. They cited an addiction to alcohol.

More prison will provide a sobering experience for a man used to the jet-set life. But the world will be watching how Steffi reacts to the verdict. She left Australia for a tournament in Japan on Friday refusing to comment. ($1=1.6383 Mark)
